questions.stem: Which equation defines density?

options.text: density = mass ÷ volume
options.explanation: Mass divided by the volume it fills.

options.text: density = volume ÷ mass
options.explanation: That inverts the relationship.

options.text: density = mass × volume
options.explanation: Multiplying has no physical meaning here.

options.text: density = weight ÷ area
options.explanation: That is pressure's territory.

questions.stem: A material's mass is measured in kilograms and its volume in metres cubed. Its density unit is

options.text: metres cubed per kilogram
options.explanation: That inverts the unit.

options.text: kilograms per metre cubed
options.explanation: The unit follows the input units directly.

options.text: grams per centimetre cubed
options.explanation: That pair belongs to gram-and-centimetre inputs.

options.text: newtons per kilogram
options.explanation: That is gravitational field strength.

questions.stem: Two identical bags hold the same volume, one filled with feathers and one with metal. What can be said about their masses?

options.text: both bags have the same density because their volumes match
options.explanation: Equal volume with different mass means different density.

options.text: neither bag has a measurable density
options.explanation: Both are perfectly measurable.

options.text: the metal bag has much the greater mass in the same volume, so the higher density
options.explanation: Equal volumes: the heavier filling is the denser material.

options.text: the feather bag is denser because feathers pile tightly
options.explanation: Feathers pack far more air between fibres.

questions.stem: Why does a gas have a lower density than the same substance as a solid?

options.text: gas particles weigh less than solid particles
options.explanation: The particles are identical; only their spacing changes.

options.text: gases have no mass at all
options.explanation: Gases are massy, just spread thin.

options.text: solid particles are always larger
options.explanation: Particle size does not change with state.

options.text: its particles are spread out, so the same mass occupies a larger volume
options.explanation: Same mass over more volume divides to a smaller density.

questions.stem: On the density formula triangle, covering V leaves

options.text: m over ρ, so V = m ÷ ρ
options.explanation: Hiding the volume exposes the mass over the density.

options.text: ρ over m, so V = ρ ÷ m
options.explanation: That inverts the rearrangement.

options.text: ρ × m, so V = ρ × m
options.explanation: That would multiply, not divide.

options.text: nothing useful — the triangle only finds density
options.explanation: The triangle serves all three rearrangements.

questions.stem: State the density equation in symbols and name each quantity with its unit.
questions.modelAnswer: ρ = m ÷ V, where ρ is the density in kilograms per metre cubed, m is the mass in kilograms and V is the volume in metres cubed.

questions.stem: State what the density of a material tells you about its mass and volume.
questions.modelAnswer: The density tells you how much mass is packed into each unit of the material's volume.

questions.stem: Explain why a balloon can occupy more space than a small lead bar yet contain far less mass.
questions.modelAnswer: Density divides mass by volume, and the balloon's filling — mostly gas — spreads very little mass through a large volume, while the lead bars cram a large mass into a small one. Occupied space alone decides nothing; the mass-per-volume ratio decides everything.

questions.stem: A cube measures 2 m along each edge and has a mass of 1600 kg. Calculate its density.
Equal-sized blocks of wood and lead: which has the greater mass?

options.text: whichever block was made first
options.explanation: History sets no mass.

options.text: the lead block, because lead is the denser material
options.explanation: Equal volumes make the density ranking decide the masses.

options.text: the wooden block, because wood is heavier grain by grain
options.explanation: Wood is the less dense material.

options.text: neither — equal sizes mean equal masses
options.explanation: Equal size does not equalise different materials.

questions.stem: Water becomes steam. What happens to the density of the water you are watching?

options.text: it stays the same — states never change density
options.explanation: State changes rearrange particle spacing dramatically.

options.text: it doubles, because steam particles split
options.explanation: Particles do not split on boiling.

options.text: it drops sharply, because the same mass now spreads through much more volume
options.explanation: Evaporation inflates the volume at constant mass.

options.text: it rises, because steam is hotter
options.explanation: Temperature alone does not set the density jump here.

questions.stem: Which statement about the three states of one substance is correct?

options.text: the gas is denser than the liquid
options.explanation: The ordering is reversed.

options.text: all three states share one density
options.explanation: Spacing changes with state, so density does too.

options.text: only the solid has any density at all
options.explanation: Every state has a measurable density.

options.text: solid and liquid are both denser than the gas state
options.explanation: The gas spreads the same mass over more volume.

questions.stem: A workshop sorts offcuts by mass alone to guess density. What must it also know?

options.text: each offcut's volume, because density compares mass to volume
options.explanation: Mass without volume prices nothing.

options.text: the offcuts' colours
options.explanation: Colour carries no density information.

options.text: the workshop's temperature only
options.explanation: Temperature is not the missing quantity here.

options.text: nothing else — mass alone fixes density
options.explanation: Density is a ratio, not a raw mass.

questions.stem: Which comparison is a fair density comparison?

options.text: a full gas jar against an empty one
options.explanation: One side has no sample to compare.

options.text: the same substance as solid versus as gas
options.explanation: One variable — the state — changes.

options.text: a balloon of helium against a bar of lead of any size
options.explanation: Both material and volume differ at once.

options.text: a warm feather against a cold anvil
options.explanation: Material, size and temperature all differ.

questions.stem: State why gases are generally less dense than solids.
questions.modelAnswer: Gas particles are more spread out, so the same mass occupies a larger volume and the mass-per-volume ratio falls.

questions.stem: State which fills a same-size bag to a greater mass: feathers or metal.
questions.modelAnswer: Metal fills the same-size bag to a far greater mass, because it is the denser material.

questions.stem: Explain why comparing the densities of two different materials is fairest when their volumes match.
questions.modelAnswer: Density is the ratio of mass to volume, so a fair material comparison holds the volume fixed and lets only the material differ. With volumes equal, the material with the greater mass is unambiguously the denser one.

questions.stem: A State changes from liquid to solid and its volume shrinks slightly while its mass stays constant. State what happens to its density.
questions.modelAnswer: The density increases, because the same mass now divides by a smaller volume.

questions.stem: Why might a density calculation need a volume formula first?

options.text: density formulas require geometry by definition
options.explanation: The density equation needs only a volume value, however obtained.

options.text: volumes are always too small to measure
options.explanation: They are measurable; the question is what is given.

options.text: the object's volume is often not stated and must come from its shape
options.explanation: Geometry supplies the missing input.

options.text: mass can only be found from volume formulas
options.explanation: Mass comes from the balance.

questions.stem: Which volume belongs to a cuboid of edges 2 m, 3 m and 4 m?

options.text: 9 m³
options.explanation: That adds the edges instead of multiplying.

options.text: 24 m²
options.explanation: Volume carries cubic units.

options.text: 12 m³
options.explanation: That drops one edge.

options.text: 24 m³
options.explanation: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 cubic metres.

questions.stem: An object's edges were measured in centimetres. What must happen before the volume feeds a kg/m³ density?

options.text: the lengths convert to metres, giving a volume in metres cubed
options.explanation: Unit discipline decides the density's unit.

options.text: nothing — centimetres feed kg/m³ directly
options.explanation: Mixed units corrupt the answer.

options.text: the mass converts to grams instead
options.explanation: The target unit is kilograms per metre cubed.

options.text: the volume converts to litres
options.explanation: Litres are not the target volume unit here.

questions.stem: A cylinder's radius and height are known. What is the shape-formula step for its volume?

options.text: add the radius to the height
options.explanation: Adding never builds a volume.

options.text: multiply π by the radius squared by the height
options.explanation: V = πr²h for a cylinder.

options.text: multiply the radius by the height
options.explanation: That misses π and the square.

options.text: cube the radius
options.explanation: Cubing suits cubes, not cylinders.

questions.stem: A slab measures 0.02 m × 0.4 m × 0.9 m and has a mass of 60 kg. Which working finds its density?

options.text: volume 1.32 m³, then 60 ÷ 1.32 ≈ 45 kg/m³
options.explanation: That adds the dimensions instead of multiplying.

options.text: density 60 × 0.0072 ≈ 0.43 kg/m³
options.explanation: Multiplying never divides mass by volume.

options.text: volume 0.0072 m³, then 60 ÷ 0.0072 ≈ 8300 kg/m³
options.explanation: The geometry feeds the division; the answer rounds to 2 s.f.
That inverts the division.

questions.stem: State the volume formula for a cube of edge length L.
questions.modelAnswer: The volume of a cube is L × L × L, the edge length cubed.

questions.stem: State what must be calculated before the density equation when the volume is not given.
questions.modelAnswer: The object's volume must be calculated from its shape using the appropriate formula first.

questions.stem: Explain why an error in the volume step propagates straight into the final density.
questions.modelAnswer: The density divides the mass by the calculated volume, so the volume sits in the denominator of the final step. Any volume error — a wrong formula, unconverted units — rescales the density directly, which is why the geometry must be written and checked before dividing.

questions.stem: A sphere of radius 0.1 m has a mass of 4.2 kg. Taking the sphere volume as 4 ÷ 3 × π × r³ and π ≈ 3, calculate its density.
